title: UFold-X: an enhanced Dual & Dynamic U-Mamba model for long-range RNA secondary structure prediction

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Listed the Google Drive folder (16 dataset pickles + 8 pretrained .pt checkpoints) and downloaded two of them: RCSB1800.cPickle (4.2 MB) and RCSB4000.cPickle (18.3 MB). Loaded both with a restricted unpickler (only numpy arrays and one named tuple inside, nothing executable) and counted: 40 records (lengths 611-1799 nucleotides, 18,012 annotated base pairs) and 61 records (lengths 2,821-4,810 nucleotides, 118,846 base pairs). Each record holds a one-hot sequence array, a per-nucleotide 3-column structure label, the length, a name that is a Protein Data Bank ID, and an explicit list of paired positions. Checked file sizes of all 16 dataset files by HTTP HEAD (4 MB to >100 MB). Read the repository code (network_small.py, ufold/data_generator.py, ufold/utils.py) and both READMEs; timed the input-feature builder (creatmat) myself: 0.84 s for a 800-nucleotide sequence, scaling as length squared (~4 s at 1,800 nt, ~33 s at 5,000 nt). Confirmed the Zenodo deposit cited in the data availability statement holds only a 74 KB code zip, no data.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All dataset sizes except the two I opened: RNAstralign 30,451 sequences split into 20,862/2,608 (<600 nt) and 8,793/1,035 (600-1,800 nt), ArchiveII 3,975 sequences, BGSU v4.4 4,494 representative RNAs, Rfam v15.0 13,859 structures, and the 12,711 RNA Mapping Database chemical-probing constructs used for the reactivity variant. All reported F1 scores, the cross-family and cross-clan benchmark results, and the 0.08 s per sequence inference time.

a1_downloadable.note: Public Google Drive folder, no login: I downloaded and parsed two dataset files. Files over ~100 MB need Drive's standard virus-scan confirm token (obtainable). Caveat: the repo README says ArchiveII and the RNAstralign-600 sets were uploaded, but the folder contains only the 1800/5000-nucleotide variants.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Verified in the files: each record carries both an explicit list of paired nucleotide positions and a per-nucleotide 3-column structure label, so the prediction target is stored, not constructed.

a3_inputs_present.note: Verified: the RNA sequence itself is stored as a one-hot array (decoded cleanly to A/U/C/G strings), so no accession lookups are needed.

a4_units_stated.note: The target is binary base pairing (position i pairs with position j), so units are not an issue; verified pair indices fall inside the stated sequence lengths.

a5_enough_rows.note: Verified only 40 + 61 = 101 structures in the two Protein Data Bank derived test sets I opened; the paper's main training source, RNAstralign, has 30,451 sequences, which is far above the threshold.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: Dataset downloads total roughly 0.5-1 GB, but the model consumes a 17-channel length x length image per sequence: 0.22 GB at 1,800 nucleotides and 1.70 GB at 5,000 nucleotides for the input tensor alone, before any network activations.
a6_fits_laptop.note: FAILS. The authors' own README states training needs about 20-40 GB of GPU memory, and reports a crash message for insufficient memory. That is above any consumer GPU and far above a 16 GB CPU-only laptop, so neither retraining the published baseline nor training a competitor is possible here. Inference on the ultra-long (2,800-5,000 nt) sets, which is the paper's entire selling point, would also exceed 16 GB of RAM once U-Net activations are added.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Verified exactly: paper says RCSB1800 = 40 sequences of 600-1,800 nt (file: 40 records, 611-1,799 nt) and RCSB4000 = 61 sequences of 2,800-5,000 nt (file: 61 records, 2,821-4,810 nt). Only mismatch is two advertised sets missing from the download folder.

a8_label_provenance.note: For the Protein Data Bank sets the base pairs were extracted by RNApdbee 2.0 from experimental 3D structures, i.e. derived from a physical measurement via standard annotation software, not from another predictor. RNAstralign/Rfam structures are comparative-analysis curations, which is the field standard but is inference from alignments rather than direct measurement.

existing_models.name: UFold-X (this paper, a dual-branch U-Net plus Mamba state-space model)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reports best F1 (harmonic mean of precision and recall over predicted base pairs) on RNAstralign-1800 and the 61-structure RCSB4000 ultra-long set, plus 'competitive and stable' performance on a new Rfam clan-level held-out split; exact numbers read from the paper text only.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Scarcity of experimentally validated structures for rare/novel RNA types, remaining homology between train and test in conventional benchmarks, no biophysical interpretability (no free-energy term), and rising memory cost from the dual-branch design.

existing_models.name: UFold (the predecessor, U-Net on base-pairing feature images)
existing_models.score_and_split: Used here as the main comparison; Szikszai et al. 2022 (Bioinformatics) retrained UFold with family-fold cross-validation and found intra-family accuracy does not carry over to unseen families.

existing_models.name: MXfold2 (deep network with thermodynamic regularisation)
existing_models.score_and_split: F1 = 0.742 on the Archive-NoFam benchmark (89 Protein Data Bank structures, 47 categories, homology-filtered) in the 2026 RNA journal benchmark; best pure deep-learning method there, still not significantly better than thermodynamic folding.

existing_models.name: SPOT-RNA / SPOT-RNA2 (deep learning with transfer learning and evolutionary profiles)
existing_models.score_and_split: SPOT-RNA F1 = 0.702 on Archive-NoFam after removing overlapping training structures (2026 RNA journal benchmark).

existing_models.name: RNA-FM and RiNALMo (RNA language models with structure heads)
existing_models.score_and_split: RNA-FM F1 = 0.710 and RiNALMo F1 = 0.544 on Archive-NoFam (2026 RNA journal benchmark).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The benchmark authors conclude no deep method substantially beats thermodynamics once homology is removed.

existing_models.name: RNAformer (axial-attention transformer with a homology-aware data pipeline)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reports state-of-the-art cross-family F1 with train/test separation built in; code and weights at github.com/automl/RNAformer (page retrieved via search, numbers not read from the paper itself).

existing_models.name: EternaFold (thermodynamic/statistical model trained on crowd-sourced chemical probing)
existing_models.score_and_split: F1 = 0.758 on Archive-NoFam, the highest of any method tested in the 2026 RNA journal benchmark, i.e. a non-deep method still leads on homology-free data.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: n/a - it is the reference others fail to beat.

backbone.name: RNA-FM (an RNA language model with open weights) would be the natural freeze-and-head backbone for per-nucleotide tasks
backbone.hardware: Pairwise contact-map prediction needs a 17 x L x L image per sequence (1.7 GB at L = 5,000) and the authors report 20-40 GB GPU memory for training; RNA-FM itself is also capped near 1,024 nucleotides, so it cannot cover the long RNAs that are the point of this paper.
backbone.licence: Paper is CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial); Zenodo code deposit is CC BY 4.0; RNA-FM and MXfold2 are open-source.

integration.partner_dataset: Protein Data Bank / RNAsolo (the record names are Protein Data Bank IDs such as 8T2S, 8EV3, verified in the files)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does predicted secondary-structure accuracy track experimental 3D resolution and RNA class, i.e. are the 'hard' long RNAs hard because of real structural complexity or because of noisy annotation? - a legitimate question, but one that still requires running the GPU-scale models.

controls.positive_control: Available in principle: a thermodynamic folder (ViennaRNA/RNAstructure) run on the same sequences must recover the canonical stems of well-studied ribosomal RNAs in these files.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the paired-position lists within each sequence and confirm F1 collapses to the dinucleotide-chance level.
controls.external_validation: Strong options exist (ArchiveII, bpRNA-new, the Archive-NoFam 89-structure set, and the Protein Data Bank entries by deposition year for a temporal split) - the evaluation side of this project is not the problem.

honest_claim_h3: A model trained on these files could claim only: 'among RNAs whose 3D structure has already been solved or whose family has a curated covariance alignment, this predicts which nucleotides pair' - a population that is heavily dominated by ribosomal and other long, highly structured RNAs and excludes the messenger RNAs and long non-coding RNAs people actually want folded.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use an RNA sequence to predict which of its nucleotides pair with which, especially for very long RNA molecules.
plain_idea.train_on: One-hot encoded RNA sequences with their annotated base pairs: 30,451 sequences in the paper's main training source (from the paper text) plus the 101 Protein Data Bank derived structures I opened and counted myself.
plain_idea.predict: A length-by-length matrix saying which nucleotide pairs with which. The true answer comes either from 3D structures solved by crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy and converted to base pairs by the RNApdbee annotation tool, or from curated evolutionary alignments.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: RNA biologists and RNA-drug designers need folded structures for long transcripts, where current tools degrade badly; a model that held up on genuinely unrelated RNA families would change which structures people trust enough to act on.

more_or_better_data.why: The data here is the field's standard benchmark collection (RNAstralign, ArchiveII, Rfam, Protein Data Bank structures) that MXfold2, SPOT-RNA, RNA-FM, RNAformer and others already train and test on; nothing new is measured.

confidence_score.why: The stored labels are binary base pairs with no replicate or confidence information; the chemical-probing reactivity data that could support calibration lives in a third-party resource (the RNA Mapping Database) and is not part of this deposit.

models_beatable.why: Seven open, reproducible models exist, and a 2026 RNA journal benchmark already evaluated five of them honestly on a homology-filtered Protein Data Bank set, where the best deep method (MXfold2, F1 = 0.742) still loses to the non-deep EternaFold (0.758). That is a crowded field with open models and honest evaluation already done.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The published baseline cannot be run as ours - retraining it needs 20-40 GB of GPU memory by the authors' own README - and no new joinable measurement is added, so the first condition fails outright.

ml_idea: The project considered was predicting the base-pairing contact map of long RNAs (600-5,000 nucleotides) from sequence, either by retraining a competitor to UFold-X or by re-evaluating the released checkpoints on a homology-aware split. It dies on compute: a 17-channel length-by-length input image is 1.7 GB per 5,000-nucleotide sequence and the authors state training needs 20-40 GB of GPU memory. The lighter fallback - per-nucleotide paired/unpaired classification from a frozen RNA language model - is both a weaker task and already covered by RNA-FM's own benchmarks, and a thermodynamic folder answers it in milliseconds.

effort.compute_note: Feature-table hours are low and real: the pickles parsed first try and expose sequence, pairs and length directly. I timed the input-feature builder on my own machine (0.84 s at 800 nucleotides, quadratic, so ~4 s at 1,800 nt) giving roughly 11 CPU-hours to featurise the ~9,800 RNAstralign-1800 sequences. Peak RAM/VRAM of 20-40 GB is the authors' stated training requirement from the repository README, not my measurement; one cross-validation run would be GPU-days and I could not time it.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read the repository README's training section - it states 20-40 GB of GPU memory and prints the out-of-memory message users should expect. Thirty seconds, and it kills the project on a CPU-only 16 GB laptop.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A6. The data itself is clean and downloadable - I opened two files and the counts matched the paper exactly (40 and 61 Protein Data Bank derived structures, with sequences and base pairs both stored) - but the model's input is a 17-channel length-by-length image (1.7 GB for one 5,000-nucleotide RNA) and the authors' own README requires 20-40 GB of GPU memory to train, so neither the published baseline nor any competitor can be run on a 16 GB CPU laptop. Secondary, independent reason: the field is saturated with open reproducible models (MXfold2, SPOT-RNA, RNA-FM, RiNALMo, RNAformer, UFold) and a 2026 RNA journal benchmark has already done the honest homology-free evaluation, finding that no deep method beats thermodynamic folding (EternaFold F1 = 0.758 versus MXfold2 0.742).
